RESUMO

Introdução: As disfunções respiratórias agudas figuram entre as principais causas de
internação em Unidades de Terapia Intensiva Pediátrica (UTIP), correspondendo a mais de um
terço das admissões e configurando-se como a forma mais prevalente de falência orgânica em
crianças criticamente enfermas. O manejo dessas condições requer domínio da mecânica
respiratória e rigor na adoção de medidas de biossegurança, especialmente em contextos de alta
transmissibilidade viral, como durante a pandemia de COVID -19. Objetivos: Integrar os
princípios da mecânica respiratória e d e biossegurança no manejo de disfunções respiratórias
agudas em UTIP, buscando estratégias que otimizem a ventilação mecânica e reduzam o risco
ocupacional para a equipe multiprofissional. Métodos: Esta tese foi composta por dois estudos
complementares. O primeiro, de caráter observacional retrospectivo, foi conduzido na UTIP do
Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre (Brasil) e incluiu 37 lactentes, de 1 a 24 meses, com
insuficiência respiratória associada a infecção viral grave e submetidos à ventilação mecânica
invasiva. O objetivo foi avaliar a relação entre a pressão inspiratória de pico (PIP) e a pressão
de platô (PPLAT), bem como a precisão de um modelo preditivo para estimativa de PPLAT a partir
da PIP. O segundo estudo, prospectivo e de coorte, foi realizado no Hospital Sainte -Justine
(Canadá) e avaliou a eficácia do dispositivo SplashGuard Caregiver (SGCG) na redução da
dispersão de aerossóis durante procedimentos geradores de aerossóis (PGA) realizados em
pacientes com COVID-19. A análise envolveu a detecção de partículas virais no ambiente e na
face de profissionais expostos a situações de alta transmissibilidade viral, sendo
complementado por simulações de dinâmica de fluidos computacional ( CFD - computational
fluid dynamycs) para analisar o comportamento aerodinâmico destas partículas. Resultados:
No primeiro estudo, observou -se que a PIP superestimou significativamente PPLAT, com
diferença média de 7,3 ± 4 cmH₂O (p < 0,01), evidenciando as limitações de modelos preditivos
baseadas apenas na PIP em lactentes com elevada resistência de vias aéreas. No segundo, a
detecção de partículas virais reduziu de 5,9% na ausência do SGCG para 3% com o uso do
dispositivo. As simulações CFD demonstraram redução de até 70% na concentração de
aerossóis suspensos no ar quando mantidas aberturas mínimas no SGCG e que o
posicionamento dos profissionais de saúde n o sentido oposto ao principal fluxo de ar do
ambiente pode promover redução adicional da exposição. Conclusões: A integração entre os
princípios da mecânica respiratória e da biossegurança fortalece a qualidade da assistência em
UTIP, favorecendo o desenvolvimento de estratégias ventilatórias mais seguras e
individualizadas, além de contribuir para a mitigação dos riscos ocupacionais.


Palavras-chave: terapia intensiva pediátrica; ventilação mecânica; mecânica respiratória;
biossegurança; COVID-19.

ABSTRACT

Introduction: Acute respiratory dysfunctions are among the leading causes of admission to
Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU), accounting for more than one third of hospitalizations
and representing the most prevalent form of organ failure in critically ill children. T he
management of these conditions requires a solid understanding of respiratory mechanics and
strict adherence to biosafety measures, particularly in settings of high viral transmissibility,
such as during the COVID-19 pandemic. Objective: To integrate the principles of respiratory
mechanics and biosafety in the management of acute respiratory dysfunctions in PICU, aiming
to develop strategies that optimize mechanical ventilation and reduce occupational risk for the
multidisciplinary healthcare team. Method: This thesis comprised two complementary studies.
The first research, a retrospective observational study, was conducted in the PICU of Hospital
de Clínicas de Porto Alegre (Brazil) and included 37 infants, aged 1 to 24 months, with
respiratory failure associated with severe viral infection who required invasive mechanical
ventilation. The objective was to assess the relationship between peak inspiratory pressure (PIP)
and plateau pressure (P PLAT), as well as to evaluate the accuracy of a predictive model for
estimating PPLAT from PIP values. The second study, a prospective cohort conducted at Sainte-
Justine Hospital (Canada), evaluated the efficacy of the SplashGuard Caregiver (SGCG) device
in reducing aerosol dispersion during aerosol -generating procedures (AGP) performed on
patients with COVID-19. The analysis involved detecting viral particles in the environment and
on the faces of healthcare workers exposed to high-transmissibility settings, complemented by
computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to examine the aerodynamic behavior of these
particles. Results: In the first study, PIP significantly overestimated PPLAT, with a mean
difference of 7.3 ± 4 cmH₂O (p < 0.01), highlighting the limitations of predictive models based
solely on PIP in infants with high airway resistance. In the second study, viral particle detection
decreased from 5.9% in the absence of the SGCG to 3% with device use. CFD simulations
demonstrated up to a 70% reduction in the concentration of airborne aerosols when minimal
openings were maintained in the SGCG and indicated that positioning healthcare professionals
opposite to the main airflow direction of the environment could further reduce exposure.
Conclusions: The integration of respiratory mechanics and bio safety principles enhances the
quality of care in the PICU, promoting the development of safer and more individualized
ventilatory strategies, while also contributing to the mitigation of occupational risks.

Keywords: pediatric intensive care; mechanical ventilation; respiratory mechanics; biosafety;
COVID-19.

1 INTRODUÇÃO

As disfunções respiratórias agudas correspondem a mais de um terço das internações
em unidade de terapia intensiva pediátrica (UTIP) e , desde 2010, representam o tipo mais
prevalente de falência orgânica (YEHYA et al. , 2022 ; KILLIEN et al. , 2023) . A ampla
diversidade etiológica — que abrange principalmente as pneumonias virais, seguidas pelas
bacterianas, pelas exacerbações de doenças pulmonares crônicas e pela síndrome do
desconforto respiratório agudo (SDRA) — exige uma abordagem individualizada e um
profundo entendimento da fisi opatologia respiratória (DE LUCA et al., 2023; COHEN et al.,
2024; DREßEN et al., 2025).
O manejo destas condições é norteado pelo suporte ventilatório, que inclui desde
oxigenioterapia, a ventilação mecânica não-invasiva (VNI) e ventilação mecânica invasiva
(VM). A gravidade do quadro associa -se a fatores de risco como prematuridade, doenças
neuromusculares, imunossupressão, cardiopatias congênitas e coinfecções bacterianas .
Pacientes com esses fatores de risco tendem a apresentar maior necessidade de VM e de tempo
de internação , constituindo justamente os grupos com maior diversidade fisiopat ológica,
representando na prática um importante desafio terapêutico (O’BRYANT et al. , 2022 ;
MAZUR; CABALLERO; NUNES, 2024). Neste cenário, a mecânica respiratória consolidou-
se como uma ferramenta essencial para o entendimento do comportamento do sistema
respiratório durante o curso de VM (PETERSON-CARMICHAEL et al., 2016).
A análise de parâmetros como complacência (C), resistência (R), pressão platô (PPLAT)
e Auto-PEEP permite identificar padrões fisiopatológicos — restritivos ou obstrutivos — e
individualizar a estratégia ventilatória. Essa avaliação é tida como chave para garantir uma
estratégia de ventilação pulmonar protetora na SDRA, a qual vem sendo associada a redução
de mortalidade e de risco de lesão pulmonar induzida pelo ventilador (ventilator-induced lung
injury – VILI) (BHALLA et al. , 2021; EMERIAUD et al., 2023; KNEYBER et al. , 2023;
BEAUCHAMP; THÉRIAULT; SAUTHIER, 2025 ). Embora amplamente estudados em
populações adultas, esses conceito s de mecânica respiratória carecem de consolidação e
validação em Pediatria, dada a expressiva diferença anatômica, a maior complacência da caixa
torácica e as demandas metabólicas específicas dessa faixa etária (TEPPER et al., 2001; SEED;
WILSON; COATES, 2012; DI CICCO et al., 2021).
Como já mencionado, os vírus desempenham um papel central nas disfunções
respiratórias, e as discussões relacionadas à contaminação viral do paciente crítico são
rotineiras. Mais recentemente, intensific ou-se também a preocupação com o risco de

contaminação da equipe multiprofissional no cuidado destes pacientes . Esse debate ganhou
destaque com o surgimento do COVID-19, especialmente em ambientes de cuidados
intensivos, onde procedimentos geradores de aerossóis (PGA) são frequentes e o contato
próximo com os pacientes é inevitável, elevando o risco ocupacional (TIAN et al., 2022).
Durante a pandemia, observou -se a implementação rigorosa de equipamentos de
proteção individual (EPI), revisão de protocolos de controle de infecção, treinamento intensivo
das equipes, fortalecimento do monitoramento epidemiológico, com impactos significativos na
redução deste risco (LEFEBVRE et al., 2023). O SplashGuard Caregiver (SGCG) – uma caixa
de acrílico instalada sobre a cabeça e o dorso dos pacientes com aberturas laterais conectadas a
pressão negativa – surge como um dispositivo adicional para reduzir o risco de contaminação
no contexto de PGA (FRANÇOIS et al., 2020). A preocupação com biossegurança também se
expandiu para outros vírus respiratórios, como o sincicial respiratório, o influenza e o rinovírus,
cujo aumento da circulação após a pandemia tem sido acompanhado por elevada frequência de
casos na UTIP (KARA et al., 2024).
Esta tese propõe, portanto, uma abordagem integrada das disfunções respiratórias
agudas em UTIP, articulando dois eixos complementares: 1) a utilização de medidas e conceitos
derivados da mecânica respiratória para otimização de VM e individualização de tratamento; e
2) a adoção de estratégias que visem reduzir os riscos ocupacionais associados à assistência
respiratória em ambientes de alta transmissibilidade viral. Seu propósito é contribuir para a
consolidação de práticas assistenciais que unam rigor científico, segurança e humanização,
fortalecendo o vínculo entre fisiologia, tecnologia e biossegurança. Para atingir esse objetivo,
o estudo foi desenvolvido em etapas su cessivas, iniciando por uma ampla revisão de
fisiopatologia/mecânica respiratória e riscos ocupacionais, seguidas pelo desenvolvimento de
um estudo observacional em mecânica respiratória e de uma coorte prospectiva em
biossegurança durante a pandemia de COVID-19.

2 REVISÃO DA LITERATURA

2.1 Disfunções Respiratórias Agudas

As disfunções respiratórias agudas estão entre as principais causas de internação e
morbimortalidade em UTIP, representando mais de um terço das admissões e correspondendo
ao tipo de falência orgânica mais prevalente em pacientes críticos (KILLIEN et al. , 2023) .
Englobam um espectro de condições clínicas caracterizadas por comprometimento da
oxigenação e /ou ventilação, cuja definição considera os diferentes graus de hipoxemia e a
necessidade de suporte ventilatório (YEHYA et al., 2023) . As principais etiologias incluem
pneumonias virais, bacterianas ou aspirativas, exacerbações de doenças pulmonares crônicas,
crises asmáticas e SDRA de causa pulmonar ou extrapulmonar (COHEN et al., 2024; DREßEN
et al., 2025).
O padrão de maturação pulmonar e imunológica é dinâmico ao longo da infância,
influenciando a resposta inflamatória e a suscetibilidade a agentes infecciosos, especialmente
aos vírus, principais causas de insuficiência respiratória aguda em pediatria (KNEYBER et al.,
2023). Em crianças, principalmente lactantes, há predominância de respostas do tipo Th2,
menor produção de interferons (especialmente IFN -γ e IFN -α), memória imunológica e
capacidade de resposta adaptativa, tornando a imunidade inata o principal mecanismo de defesa
inicial contra vírus respiratórios (LAMBERT; CULLEY, 2017; HEINONEN et al. , 2019;
VERHOEVEN, 2019). A resposta inflamatória pode ser desregulada, com produção excessiva
de citocinas pró-inflamatórias (IL-6, IL-1β), menor eficiência na eliminação viral e ambiente
imunológico tolerogênico, o que contribui para quadros mais graves e recorrentes de pneumonia
viral, com risco aumentado de sobreposição bacteriana (COATES et al., 2015; JONES et al.,
2019)
A presença de disfunções respiratórias agudas associa-se a piores desfechos, incluindo
risco de evolução para SDRA, aumento do tempo de VM e a maior incidência de falência de
múltiplos órgãos que corresponde ao principal fator independente de mortalidade em crianças
com insuficiência respiratória aguda (LÓPEZ-FERNÁNDEZ et al., 2012). A SDRA pediátrica
representa uma entidade de elevada complexidade diagnóstica e terapêutica com incidência de
apenas 3%, mas elevada taxa de mortalidade chegando a até 17% (KHEMANI et al., 2019).
Desde a definição do Pediatric Acute Lung Injury Consensus Conference (PALICC), em 2015,
houve importante avanço na padronização de critérios diagnósticos, estratificação de gravidade
e aplicação de estratégias ventilatórias protetoras adaptadas à população pediátrica (JOUVET

15
et al., 2015; EMERIAUD et al., 2023). Entretanto, persiste uma lacuna entre o conhecimento
teórico e a incorporação sistemática dessas práticas na rotina clínica, especialmente em
contextos de alta demanda e recursos limitados (BHALLA et al., 2021).
O manejo das disfunções respiratórias em pediatria deve considerar a diversidade
anatômica e funcional das diferentes faixas etárias, que influenciam diretamente a mecânica
respiratória e a resposta à VM (TRACHSEL et al., 2022; KNEYBER et al., 2023). A maior
complacência da parede torácica, o calibre reduzido das vias aéreas, a menor reserva funcional
e o consumo metabólico elevado tornam o sistema respiratório pediátrico particularmente
vulnerável à fadiga muscular e à hipoxemia sustentada (DI CICCO et al., 2021).

2.2 Repercussão da Disfunções Respiratórias no Paciente Pediátrico – Mecânica Respiratória

A mecânica respiratória fundamenta-se na interação entre pressão, volume e fluxo no
sistema respiratório, sendo regida por propriedades físicas que incluem complacência,
elastância, resistência e trabalho respiratório (KAMINSKY; COCKCROFT; DAVIS, 2023).
Esses elementos constituem a base fisiológica para a compreensão tanto da respiração
espontânea, em que o gradiente de pressão é gerado pela ação dos músculos respiratórios,
quanto da ventilação mecânica, na qual a pressão positiva aplicada pelo ventilador modifica os
determinantes da distensão pulmonar e da movimentação de ar (GRINNAN; TRUWIT, 2005).
A avaliação da mecânica respiratória pode ser realizada por métodos como
espirometria, oscilometria, técnicas de interrupção do fluxo e manometria esofágica, sendo que
a escolha do método depende da idade e da capacidade de cooperação da criança (ARETS;
VAN DER ENT, 2004; BOAS; REN , 2025) . Em pacientes críticos, a análise da mecânica
respiratória é feita através do próprio ventilador mecânico e é fundamental para ajustar
estratégias ventilatórias, monitorar a evolução clínica e minimizar lesão pulmonar induzida pela
ventilação (HESS, 2014; PETERSON-CARMICHAEL et al., 2016; ANDREOLIO et al., 2021;
CRUCES, 2023 ). A Tabela 1 resume as principais variáveis de mecânica respiratória que
permitem identificar padrões fisiopatológicos (restritivos e obstrutivos) e individualizar a
estratégia ventilatória.
O conceito de lesão pulmonar induzida pela ventilação (VILI, ventilator-induced lung
injury) engloba diferentes mecanismos de dano, incluindo barotrauma, volutrauma,
atelectrauma, biotrauma e ergotrauma, e tem sido amplamente discutido nos últimos anos .
Estratégias de ventilação protetora – que derivam diretamente dos princípios da mecânica
respiratória – voltadas à limitação do stress (variação de pressão) e d o strain (deformação

16
pulmonar representada pelo volume corrente) – buscando evitar tanto o colapso alveolar quanto
hiperdistensão, constituem pilares fundamentais para a redução da VILI (GATTINONI et al.,
2017). Entre as práticas recomendadas na VM protetora em SDRA tem -se: limitação de
volumes correntes (V T), pressão platô (P PLAT), Driving Pressure (DP) e titulação de pressão
expiratória final positiva (PEEP) de acordo com FiO 2 considerando as melhores respostas de
complacência estática do sistema respiratório (CST) e da DP (EMERIAUD et al., 2023).
O uso rotineiro de medidas de mecânica respiratória na UTIP permanece limitado por
dificuldades técnicas, pela grande variabilidade dos tamanhos corporais e pela ausência de
conceitos consolidados e validados especificamente para a população pediátrica (PETERSON-
CARMICHAEL et al. , 2016) . Além disso, a maioria dos estudos de mecânica respiratória
conduzidos em adultos, foi realizada em pacientes ventilados em modo volume controlado, na
ausência de esforço respiratório espontâneo e de hiperinsuflação dinâmica, condições
necessárias para a obtenção adequada de PPLAT e CST, enquanto a titulação de PEEP se deu em
modo pressão controlada (HESS, 2014; AMATO et al., 2015).
No contexto pediátrico, observa -se predominância do uso de modos ventilatórios de
fluxo desaceleração, ou seja, pressão controlada e pressão regulada volume controlado, nos
quais a PPLAT é raramente medida, sendo frequentemente substituída por pressão inspiratória de
pico (PIP) (PANICO et al. , 2015 ; BHALLA et al. , 2021) . Embora alguns estudos tenham
demonstrado boa correlação entre PIP e PPLAT em crianças com doença pulmonar restritiva e
mediana de idade de 8,6 anos, a realidade da UTIP inclui um grande contingente de lactentes
com importante componente obstrutivo, condição em que essa correlação tende a ser menos
precisa (BURATTI; PIVA; JOUVET, 2022; PATEL; THOMAS; YEHYA, 2022).

2.3 Repercussão das disfunções respiratórias na equipe assistencial

2.3.1 Riscos ocupacionais na assistência respiratória

O ambiente da UTI P é caracterizado pela exposição da equipe multiprofissional a
riscos ocupacionais elevados, especialmente em períodos de alta transmissibilidade viral —
como durante a pandemia de COVID -19, surtos de influenza, vírus sincicial respiratório e
outros patógenos respiratórios (BANSAL et al. , 2025) . A Organização Mundial da Saúde
estimou que profissionais da saúde representaram cerca de 11% dos casos notificados de
COVID-19, com variações entre países de acordo com a capacidade de testagem . A taxa de
contaminação foi maior entre aqueles que atuavam em terapia intensiva – odds ratio 2,17 (IC
95%: 1,01–4,68) – e expostos a procedimentos gerados de aerossóis, com odds ratio 1,36 (IC
95%: 1,21–1,52) (GÓMEZ-OCHOA et al., 2021; NASA et al., 2022; BANSAL et al., 2025).
Gotículas são partículas respiratórias expelidas ao falar, tossir ou espirrar, com
diâmetro > 5 μm, que tendem a se depositar rapidamente por gravidade e geralmente alcançam
distâncias inferiores a 1–2 metros. Em contraste, aerossóis têm diâmetro < 5 μm, p ermanecem
suspensos no ar por períodos prolongados, dispersam -se por distâncias maiores e apresentam
maior probabilidade de serem inalados profundamente nas vias aéreas (SIEGEL et al., 2007).
Evidências recentes demonstram que a maior parte das partículas expelidas durante respiração,
fala ou procedimentos médicos são aerossóis, e que a transmissão ocorre predominantemente a
curta distância devido à alta concentração próxima à fonte emissora (FENNELLY, 2020).
Procedimentos geradores de aerossóis (PGA) são definidos como intervenções
médicas que produzem partículas respiratórias suficientemente pequenas (<5 μm) para
permanecerem suspensas no ar por tempo prolongado, aumentando o risco de transmissão de
patógenos respiratórios em ambientes hospitalares (SIEGEL et al., 2007). Entre eles incluem-
se intubação ou extubação, aspiração de vias aéreas, ventilação não invasiva, reanimação
cardiopulmonar, broncoscopia e administração de medicamentos nebulizados (TRAN et al.,
2012). Além desses fatores, estudos recentes ressaltam que o risco de transmissão também é
influenciado pelo contexto clínico, pela carga viral do paciente, pela proximidade física e pelas
condições de ventilação do ambiente (NASA et al., 2022; THURESSON et al., 2022).
Mais especificamente em UTIP, a combinação entre a alta frequência de
procedimentos geradores de aerossóis e o contato próximo com pacientes pediátricos — que
frequentemente choram, tossem e têm menor capacidade de cooperar com barreiras físicas —

19
parece aumentar substancialmente o risco ocupacional quando comparado a outros setores
hospitalares (HE et al., 2017).

2.3.2 Estratégias de biossegurança

A implementação de práticas rigorosas de biossegurança mostrou-se determinante para
a redução de infecções ocupacionais . Essas práticas incluem: (1) estratégias de proteção
individual, (2) controle ambiental com ventilação adequada, (3) otimização da engenharia dos
ventiladores, minimizando ao máximo vazamentos, e (4) organização de fluxos assistenciais
(KLOMPAS et al., 2021).
O uso adequado e consistente de equipamentos de proteção individual (EPI) envolve
a utilização de máscaras N95 durante procedimentos geradores de aerossóis ou em períodos de
alta incidência de vírus respiratórios, enquanto as cirúrgicas podem ser empregadas em
situações de menor risco. Além disso, a proteção ocular, avental e luvas são recomendados para
o contato com qualquer paciente portador de infecção respiratória (NASA et al. , 2022;
ZANELLA; RHEE; KLOMPAS, 2025).
As diretrizes da American Heart Association (2025) reforçam o uso rigoroso de EPI
— incluindo proteção respiratória (N95 ou equivalente), proteção ocular, luvas e avental —
durante a realização de procedimentos geradores de aerossóis em pacientes com patógenos
respiratórios de alto risco, como COVID -19 e influenza (CAO et al. , 2025) . A vacinação
universal de profissionais e pacientes elegíveis contra influenza e COVID -19 constitui
estratégia comprovada para reduzir a transmissão e a gravidade das infecções (ZANELLA;
RHEE; KLOMPAS, 2025).
A pandemia de COVID-19 impulsionou a adoção de novos protocolos de segurança ,
incluindo filtros de ar de alta eficiência (HEPA - High-Efficiency Particulate Air) nos circuitos
respiratórios, modificações nas interfaces de ventilação, realização de procedimentos em salas
com pressão negativa e o SGCG (JOUVET; AUBIN, [s. d.]; MONROE et al., 2022; CAO et
al., 2025). Este último corresponde a uma caixa de acrílico colocada sobre a cabeça e o tronco
do paciente com aberturas laterais que permitem o atendimento e que após permanecem
fechadas e conectadas a pressão negativa (Figura 1 ) (FRANÇOIS et al. , 2020) . Ainda,
recomenda-se limitar o número de profissionais presentes durante os procedimentos e otimizar
a ventilação ambiental, uma vez que a proximidade do paciente, a elevada carga viral e a
ventilação inadequada são fatores críticos para a transmissão aérea (THURESSON et al., 2022;
UYEKI et al., 2022).

2.4. Integração entre mecânica respiratória e biossegurança

A segurança do paciente em UTIP compreende diversas esferas de cuidado, com
destaque para a ventilação pulmonar protetora, a prevenção de pneumonia associada à VM e o
manejo criterioso das sedações, visando minimizar quadros de delirium e abstinência
(KLOMPAS et al., 2022; SMITH et al., 2022; KNEYBER et al., 2023). Essas estratégias são
complementadas por medidas de prevenção de eventos adversos e de controle de
infecção/biossegurança (SIEGEL et al., D’ERRICO et al., 2022). Um dos focos desta tese é a
integração de dois pilares essenciais na segurança do paciente: a mecânica pulmonar e a
biossegurança.
Através de uma análise sistemática da mecânica respiratória, torna -se possível
identificar fenótipos fisiopatológicos distintos, como os padrões obstrutivos ou restritivos, que
orientam a individualização dos ajustes ventilatórios. Esse manejo ocorre frequentemente em

21
contextos em que a realização de procedimentos geradores de aerossóis (PGA) é inevitável .
Nesse cenário, a implementação de intervenções que reduzam a dispersão de partículas torna -
se essencial, sendo o dispositivo SGCG uma estratégia possível visando um ambiente mais
protegido, sem a necessidade de interromper a continuidade do cuidado do paciente crítico.
Essa articulação entre a fisiologia respiratória, a ventilação protetora e as práticas de
biossegurança configuram um modelo ampliado de segurança na UTIP. Tal modelo reforça que
a qualidade da assistência respiratória não se restringe apenas ao ajuste técnico de parâmetros
no ventilador, mas depende da criação de um ambiente assistencial seguro que viabilize a
execução dessas estratégias. Ao conectar esses conceitos, é possível avançar para um modelo
de cuidado que seja, simultaneamente, eficiente, individualizado e sustentável para o paciente
pediátrico crítico.

3 JUSTIFICATIVA

As disfunções respiratórias agudas constituem uma das principais causas de internação
e mortalidade em unidade de terapia intensiva pediátrica . Apesar dos avanços no suporte
ventilatório, o manejo desses pacientes ainda enfrenta importantes desafios relacionados à
heterogeneidade da fisiopatologia pulmonar e à escassez de evidências específicas para a
população infantil. A compreensão e o uso si stemático da mecânica respiratória têm se
mostrado como uma das ferramentas fundamentais para a individualização d a ventilação
mecânica e para a redução de complicações associadas.
Paralelamente, a realidade assistencial em unidade de terapia intensiva pediátrica tem
sido marcada por cenários de alta transmissibilidade viral, nos quais a segurança da equipe de
saúde torna -se um componente indissociável da qualidade do cuidado. Situações como a
pandemia de COVID-19 evidenciaram a vulnerabilidade dos profissionais expostos a aerossóis
durante a assistência e a necessidade de equilibrar medidas de biossegurança com a
continuidade do atendimento crítico.
Assim, esta tese se justifica pela necessidade de compreender, sistematizar e propor
modelos que articulem o conhecimento científico da mecânica respiratória com práticas de
biossegurança, contribuindo para a evolução das práticas assistenciais e para a fo rmação de
equipes mais conscientes e protegidas.

5.1 MÉTODOS - ARTIGO 1

O estudo teve delineamento observacional retrospectivo e foi conduzido na Unidade
de Terapia Intensiva Pediátrica do Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre vinculado a
Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul , com aprovação do Comitê de Ética (CAAE
44889114.7.0000.5327). Foram incluídos dados de mecânica respiratória de lactentes de 1 a 24
meses internados entre maio de 2017 e dezembro de 2021 por falência respiratória aguda
decorrente de infecção respiratória viral grave e submetidos à ventilação mecânica invasiva.
Os dados de mecânica respiratória utilizados nesta tese são provenientes dos bancos
vinculados ao projeto de pesquisa intitulado “Valores da Mecânica Pulmonar de Crianças e
Adolescentes Submetidos à Ventilação Mecânica”, aprovado pelo Comitê de Ética em Pesquisa
do Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre em julho de 2015 descrito acima. Em janeiro de 2022,
foi submetida e posteriormente aprovada uma emenda (Emenda nº 1) com o objetivo de incluir
novos dados de mecânica respiratória coletados rotineiramente durante o inverno de 2021.
A amostra incluiu pacientes com diagnóstico clínico e radiológico compatível com
infecção respiratória viral grave, teste viral positivo e disponibilidade de ao menos uma
mensuração completa de mecânica respiratória entre 6 e 48 horas após a intubação. Foram
excluídos pacientes com doença pulmonar crônica, cardiopatias congênitas não corrigidas,
aqueles com presença de drenos torácicos, traqueostomia ou fuga aérea superior a 15%.
A ventilação mecânica foi conduzida nos modos pressão controlada ou pressão
regulada volume controlado, seguindo protocolo institucional previamente estabelecido, com

25
parâmetros de referência: frequência respiratória ≤ 20 incursões respiratórias por minuto, tempo
inspiratório de 0,75–0,90 segundos, volume corrente de 8 –10 mL/kg e PEEP de 3 –5 cmH₂O.
Para mensuração das variáveis respiratórias, assegurou-se ausência de esforço respiratório
espontâneo e o s pacientes foram temporariamente colocados em modo volume controlado

A análise estatística contemplou avaliação de normalidade (teste de Kolmogorov –

Etapa 1:
Coorte prospectiva: realizada entre abril e junho de 2021, na UTIP do Hospital Sainte-

acabaram utilizando leitos de UTIP em contexto de pandemia e os profissionais de saúde

Os PGA analisados incluíram intubação e extubação orotraqueal, aspiração

Em relação a análise estatística, os dados qualitativos foram expressos em frequências

Driving pressure ( ΔP = plateau pressure [P PLAT] minus positive end -expiratory
pressure [PEEP]) has generated increasing interest in recent years since it is considered the
measure that best stratifies mortality risk in critically ill adults with acute respiratory distress
syndrome (ARDS) (1). Conseque ntly, ΔP is a potential predictor of ventilator -induced lung
injury and a possible target to define the safety limits of mechanical ventilation (2, 3). In
children, similar results have recently been published: Díaz et al (4) reported that ΔP is the
formula that best discriminated patients with pediatric ARDS (PARDS) from those without,
and van Schelven et al (5) showed that ΔP was independently associated with increased time to
extubation.
PPLAT measurement is performed in adults in the static condition when gas flow reaches
zero using the volume -controlled mode (1). Contrasting with adult critical care, pressure-
controlled modes with decelerating flow are predominantly used in the PICU (6), and peak
inspiratory pressure (PIP) is used in some studies to estimate PPLAT in PARDS for ΔP
calculation (7–9). In this issue of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine, Patel et al (10) address a
knowledge gap in the reliability of PPLAT estimation using PIP in pressure-controlled mode. The
authors show that in a cohort of 52 patients with PARDS (median age of 8.6 yr old [3.2 –16.0
yr old]), PIP was close to PPLAT measured in the static condition, that is, PIP was 1.0 ± 0.6 cm
H2O above PPLAT (95% limits of agreement of -0.3 to 2.2). Therefore, Patel et al (10) concluded
that PIP measured during decelerating flow ventilation may be an adequate surrogate of PPLAT
in PARDS when inspiratory flow approaches zero.
This new study by Patel et al (10) is well designed, including a cohort of PARDS
children with an oxygenation index of 15.7 (9.0 –21.0) and bilateral infiltrates on chest
radiograph. In such a cohort, inspiratory airway resistance (R AW) is most likely low, which is
the ideal condition for a zero-flow plateau at the end of inspiratory time. Indeed, the inspiratory
time constant ( τ) in such circumstances is estimated to be 0.04 seconds. That is, since τ =
respiratory system compliance × RAW, which is the same as this equation: (VT [mL/kg] × weight

29
[kg])/(PPLAT – PEEP) (cmH 2O) × R (cmH 2O/L/s) (11). τ is arrived at by using median tidal
volume = 6.4 mL/kg, mean body weight = 27 kg at 8.6 years old (12), PPLAT = 29.5 cmH2O,
PEEP = 12cm H 2O (see article Supplemental Table in reference [10]), normal inspiratory
resistance = 4 cmH2O/L/s (13). As zero flow is obtained at five time constants (≈ 0.2s) (11), an
inspiratory time set at more than 0.8 seconds (see the Supplemental Table in reference [10])
guarantees a prolonged period of time at zero flow and explains the quality of the current results.
Two main factors increase RAW, and thus time constant, and lead to a lower correlation
between PIP in the pressure-controlled mode and Pplat: age and respiratory diseases. Young
age is associated with higher RAW mainly because of narrower airways. For example, normal
values of RAW are 40 cmH2O/L/s at birth, 15 cmH2O/L/s at 1 year old, and 4 cmH2O/L/s at 7
years old (i.e., 10 -fold lower than the value at birth) (13). Hence, the longer time constant in
younger children, who generally also have shorter inspiratory time. As one -third of children
admitted to PICU are under 1 year old (14), the general izability of the current results (10),
which included older children, requires more investigation. Many respiratory diseases increase
RAW. When we do not have RAW measurements available, it is still possible to qualitatively
assess the presence of increased RAW by using the respiratory disease classification of the
Pediatric Mechanical Ventilation Consensus Conference, that is, normal lung, restrictive,
obstructive airway, and mixed respiratory diseases (15).
Taking all of the above together, in the absence of PPLAT measurement in the static
condition, estimation of PPLAT from dynamic measurements needs to also consider the resistive
component. Much remains to be learned about the best ventilatory strategies in children,
particularly with respect to protective ventilation: Do we need to target an optimal ΔP to im-
prove outcomes? Does the age of the child alter the ΔP target? What is the impact of the
respiratory disease on the ΔP goal? By offering a better unde rstanding of the respiratory
mechanics of critically ill children in different disease phenotypes, we should be able to answer
these questions in the future.

Artigo 1: The lack of accuracy of peak inspiratory pressure to estimate plateau pressure in
infants with severe obstructive lower airway disease.
Publicado no: Pediatric Pulmonology em agosto de 2024.
DOI: 10.1002/ppul.27245.
Número de citações: 3.

Abstract
Purpose: In children with acute respiratory distress syndrome receiving mechanical ventilation,
the peak inspiratory pressure (PIP) is close to plateau pressure (P PLAT) when inspiratory flow
approaches zero. We aimed to evaluate the reliability of PIP to estimate P PLAT in infants with
severe respiratory viral infection (SRVI), characterized by increased airway resistance, and the
accuracy of an equational model to estimates PPLAT (ePPLAT) based on PIP.
Methods: This was a retrospective observational study including mechanically ventilated
children (1 to 24 month old) with SRVI, whose respiratory mechanics measurements were
performed to evaluate PIP and PPLAT. The measured PPLAT was compared with the result of the
equation: ePPLAT = PIP – [5.067 – (0.858 × static compliance) – (0.018 × inspiratory resistance)
– (0.390 × pressure above positive-end expiratory pressure) + (4.989 × inspiratory time)].
Results: Thirty-seven patients were included, with a median age of 3 (2 –5) months. They
presented a high inspiratory and expiratory resistance (136 ± 43 and 168 ± 66 cmH 2O/L/s,
respectively) and a moderate reduction in static compliance: 0.75 ± 0.3 mL/kg/cmH2O. PIP
overestimated PPLAT (33 ± 3 and 26 ± 5 cmH 2O, p = 0.01), with a mean difference of 7.3 ± 4
cmH2O. Moreover, the Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean difference between PPLAT
and ePPLAT of 1.0±4.0 cmH2O, with 95% limits of agreement of –6.9 and 8.8.
Conclusions: A large difference between PIP and P PLAT was observed in infants with SRVI as
well as the equation model was inaccurate to estimated P PLAT based on PIP. Any estimation of
PPLAT from PIP needs to consider the resistive component of respiratory system.

Introduction
Plateau pressure (PPLAT) is the pressure applied by a mechanical ventilator to the small
airways and alveoli. In the absence of patient effort, PPLAT reflects transpulmonary pressure
and, depending on its values, may be associated with ventilation -induced lung injury (VILI).
Thus, limiting PPLAT represents a key principle in lung -protective ventilation in patients with
acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)1. The 2023 Pediatric Acute Lung Injury Consensus
Conference (PALICC -2)2 proposed limiting PPLAT, tidal volume (V T), and driving pressure

32
(P), the latter corresponding to the ratio between V T and static compliance (C ST), calculated
at the bedside as PPLAT minus positive-end expiratory pressure (PEEP).
Despite the lack of data on lung mechanics in pediatric patients, it is reasonable to infer
that monitoring physiologic lung variables (e.g.: lung compliance and airway pressures) would
be helpful to guide safer mechanical ventilation strategies. However, only recently data on pul-
monary mechanics have been further explored, both in bench models and in different clinical
populations, and predominantly in conditions of reduced compliance and /or increased
resistance
3-6
. Therefore , different ventilation modes and mechanical ventilator models have
been used, with the aim of understanding the behavior of lung mechanics in pediatric patients
and how their use could be better applied in clinical practice.
Pulmonary compliance estimates the elasticity of the respiratory system, correlating
the VT to the pressure required to introduce it into the lungs. It can be measured statically (CST),
which considers the elasticity of the lungs and chest compartment at rest (zero flow), using the
formula CST = VT/PPLAT minus PEEP, or its dynamic measurement (C D), which also considers
airway resistance, using the formula CD = VT/positive inspiratory pressure (PIP) minus PEEP.
Pulmonary resistance (RAW) corresponds to the combined resistance from airways, lung tissue,
and the endotracheal tube in invasive mechanical ventilation and is also influenced by the
patient's spontaneous breathing. It can be calculated as R = PIP minus P PLAT/Flow (inspiratory
or expiratory)7,8.
Regarding PPLAT, it is usually measured in volume control mode during an inspiratory
pause, when the inspiratory flow approaches zero in a patient without respiratory effort 9. In
children receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), pressure -regulated volume control
(PRVC) or pressure control (PC) are the most frequently used ventilation modes10, in which the
flow and volume will vary according to the patient's respiratory mechanics and effort.
Therefore, even with an inspiratory pause and absence of patient effort, p eak inspiratory
pressure (PIP) will be similar to P PLAT only if the inspiratory time (TI) is long enough to reach
zero flow 11. However, in volume -controlled (VC) mode, the pressure varies according to
respiratory mechanics, as the ventilator delivers a predefined V T using the same flow -time
waveform in every breath. Thus, during the inspiratory pause, the airway pressure will drop
until it reaches P PLAT, regardless of inspiratory time 11. Recent data from a group of pediatric
patients with ARDS showed excell ent agreement between P PLAT and P measurements,
regardless of the ventilator mode used6,12.

33
In general, PPLAT is rarely measured in children, and PIP has been adopted as the main
pressure parameter monitored 13. Nonetheless, PIP is known to be significantly influenced by
the Resistance properties of the respiratory system and may overestimate P PLAT3. The child's
age and underlying respiratory disease are the main factors associated with increased R AW and
may lead to a poor correlation between PIP and PPLAT. For instance, RAW decreases with age as
airway size increases (40 cmH 2O.L
-1
.s at birth, 15 cmH 2O.L
-1
.s at 1 ye ar old [yo], and 4
cmH2O.L
-1
.s at 7 yo14), but increases in cases of airway narrowing such as in severe respiratory
viral infection (SRVI)4,5.
Given that one-third of children admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU)
are under 2 yo and SRVI is the leading cause of admission in this age group 15, we aimed to
assess the reliability of PIP for estimating PPLAT and whether a proposed in vitro model3 would
be able to estimate PPLAT from PIP in infants.


Methods
Study design and patient selection: This retrospective observational study was
approved by the Institutional Review Board of Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre (CAAE
44889114.7.0000.5327). Informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the
study, which involved routinely co llected data. We included patients admitted to the PICU
between May 2017 and December 2021 who met the following criteria: (1) acute respiratory
failure requiring IMV; (2) diagnosis of SRVI based on classic symptoms of acute viral illness,
chest radiograph showing typical signs of pulmonary hyperinflation associated or not with areas
of consolidation, atelectasis and bronchoalveolar infiltrate, and a confirmed viral screening test;
(3) age between 1 month and 2 years; and (4) at least one measurement of respiratory mechanics
between 6 and 48 h after intubation. The following exclusion criteria were used: (1) chronic
lung or airway disease; (2) uncorrected congenital heart disease; (3) chest or mediastinal drains
considering possible air leaks; (4) tracheostomy; and (5) endotracheal tube air leak >15%
[(inspiratory tidal volume minus expiratory tidal volume/ inspiratory tidal volume) × 100].
SRVI management and data collection : IMV support was administered using the
Maquet® SERVO I ventilator, and the ventilatory modes used were PRVC and PC. The SRVI
IMV management protocol, previously published elsewhere 16, included the following
parameters: low respiratory rate (RR à 20 breaths/minute), T I between 0.75 and 0.90s, V T
between 8 and 10 mL/kg of ideal body weight, and positive end -expiratory pressure (PEEP)

34
between 3 and 5 cmH2O. Demographics, laboratory and radiologic data, ventilator settings, and
respiratory mechanics parameters were collected from medical records. After confirmation that
the patient had no spontaneous respiratory effort (RR from the patient is equal to the RR setting
in the ventilator), the ventilatory mode was switched to VC, with some exhaled VT maintained
and all other settings unchanged, for routine measurement of P PLAT. If the patient exhibited
spontaneous ventilation effort, the medical staff made individu alized decisions regarding the
best strategy to obtain measurements in static mode (without interference from voluntary
respiratory efforts). In some cases, the ventilator's respiratory rate was temporarily increased
(to elevate minute ventilation) and/or an additional dose of sedative was administered . Then,
inspiratory and expiratory pauses were performed, both with a maximum duration of 5 s, and
zero flow was confirmed by graphic evaluation in the ventilator. During the inspiratory pause,
CST, inspiratory resistance (R I), and P PLAT were measured, while total PEEP and expiratory
resistance (RE) were recorded during the expiratory pause.
Assessment of the reliability of an in vitro model to estimate plateau pressure: Ilia
et al.3 described the following equation based on a bench test model: estimated PPLAT (ePPLAT)
= PIP – [5.067 - (0.858 × C) - (0.018 × RAW) – (0.390 × pressure above PEEP) + (4.989 × TI)].
This model was compared to the in vivo measurements obtained in our study, in which we used
the absolute value of C ST, i.e, not divided by weight, R AW as RI, and pressure above PEEP as
PIP minus PEEP.
Statistical analysis: Data are expressed as absolute values, percentages, mean ( with
standard deviation), or median ( with interquartile range). The Kolmogorov -Smirnov test was
used to determine normality. The paired t -test was performed to evaluate the difference in the
means of PIP and P PLAT. Pearson correlation (r), coefficient of determination (r 2), and Bland-
Altman analyses were used to describe the agreement between PIP and PPLAT and between PPLAT
and ePPLAT. Moreover, a multivariate analysis was performed to estimate PPLAT from PIP using
our data. The level of significance was p -value ≤ 0.05. Spreadsheet, statistical analyses, and
graphs were generated using SPSS, version 28.0.


Results
Thirty-seven subjects were included (Table 1) with a median age of 3.0 months (2.0 –
5.0), a Pediatric Index of Mortality 2 of 0.2% (0.2 – 0.5), and an oxygen saturation index of 4.0
(3.6 – 4.8). A causal virus was identified in 31 (83.8%) subjects, associated bacterial pneumonia

35
accounted for sixteen (43.2%) cases, and two (5.4%) patients developed pediatric acute
respiratory distress syndrome (PARDS) according to the PALICC definition17.
Mean RI and RE were elevated (136 ± 43 and 168 ± 66 cmH2O.L
-1
.s, respectively) with
a moderate decrease in C ST (0.75 ± 0.3 cmH2O.L
-1
.s). The resulting median inspiratory time
constant (CT = CST x RI) was 0.49 seconds (0.42 – 0.72) with a TI of 0.80 (0.80 – 0.85) seconds
and an RR of 18 (18 – 20) breaths/minute.
We observed that PIP (33 ± 3 cmH2O) overestimated PPLAT (26 ± 5 cmH2O, p < 0.001)
with a moderate correlation (r = 0.57, p < 0.001 and r2 = 0.33, p < 0.001) and a mean difference

panel A).
We found a moderate correlation (r = 0.55 and r2 = 0.30) between ePPLAT 25 ± 5 cmH2O
and PPLAT 26 ± 5 cmH2O. The Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean difference between
PPLAT and ePPLAT of 1.0 ± 4.0 cmH 2O with 95% limits of agreement (LOA) of – 6.9 and 8.8
(Figure 1, panel B ). In addition, a multivariate analysis was performed with the following
variables from our sample: C ST, RI, TI and pressure above PEEP. The purpose was to provide

Discussion
Based on objective measurements of respiratory mechanics in infants with SRVI, we
found that the difference between PIP and PPLAT can be as high as 14 cmH2O, which is mainly
due to the increased resistance in components of the respiratory system. Additionally, the
equation proposed by Ilea et al.3 was not sufficiently accurate to estimate PPLAT from PIP in this
group of patients.

38
Patel et al.12 reported that, in children with PARDS (mean age 8.6 years), PIP could
be a reasonable substitute for P PLAT, as long as the inspiratory flow reaches zero. R AW was
probably low in that cohort, which created favorable conditions for accurate P PLAT estimation.
The estimated inspiratory time constant in their study was 0.04s18 Considering that zero flow is
achieved after five -time constants, 19 a TI higher than 0.80 s12 would ensure adequate time at
zero flow and explain the quality of the results. In contrast, in our study, the time constant was
10 times higher (0.49 s), and T I was 0.80 s. Even with IMV parameters optimized for the
underlying disease, zero flow cannot be guaranteed to achieve a strong agreement between
PPLAT and PIP.
Furthermore, we searched for a model to estimate PPLAT from PIP. Using the equation
proposed by Ilia et al.,3 we obtained a moderate correlation between PP LAT and ePPLAT, with a
mean difference of 1.0 ± 4.0 mmHg and large LOA. Moreover, while the in vitro equation by
Ilia et al. 3 achieved an adjusted r 2 of 0.84, we only obtained a value of 0.34 using the same
variables, which significantly limits external validation. This discrepancy may be related to the
complexity of reproducing the variability of differe nt lung mechanics scenarios in a bench
model, as well as to the fact that we tested the eP PLAT equations on a homogenous population
with a small sample size.
The scientific evidence supports maintaining spontaneous ventilatory efforts during
IMV, even in patients with severe lung diseases. However, from our perspective, it seems more
reasonable to measure respiratory variables in static mode, as it is less subj ect to bias. More
accurate data on respiratory physiology helps classify and quantify different types of lung
diseases (e.g.: restrictive, obstructive or mixed) and select the safest mode of mechanical
ventilation.
We are aware that this study has some limitations. Conducting the study in a single
center may have introduced some inherent biases, such as: local characteristics (e.g.: virus
epidemiology and/or genetic pattern of this sample) and severity of lung disease in this sample.
Despite these considerations, we believe our results clearly highlight the importance of airway
resistance when estimating PPLAT in young children with SRVI.
Clinical research into PARDS has enhanced lung -protective ventilation strategies,
including the monitoring of driving pressure. 6,20 In patients with SRVI, the next step is to use
PPLAT and other pulmonary mechanics parameters to monitor disease progression, provide
objective markers of disease reversibility, and inform the decision-making process for initiating
weaning.

39
Conclusion
In this study, we demonstrated that in infants with SRVI, manifested by elevated
inspiratory and expiratory respiratory resistance, there is a significant difference between PIP
and PPLAT. Additionally, the equation model based on PIP lacked accuracy to estimated P PLAT.
We recommend that, particularly in young children with SRVI, any attempt to estimate PPLAT
from PIP consider the resistance component of respiratory system.

Methods: This prospective observational study investigated HCWs caring for patients with
SARS-CoV-2 admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU). Rooms were categorized as: SGCG
present and SGCG absent. Virus detection was performed through direct analysis and using a
CFD model to simulate the movement dynamics of airborne particles produced by a patient’s
respiratory activities.
Findings: Of the 67 analyses performed, three samples tested positive on quantitative
polymerase chain reaction: one of 33 analyses in the SCCG group (3%) and two of 34 analyses
in the non-SGCG group (5.9%). CFD simulations showed that: (1) reduction of th e gaps of an
SGCG could decrease the number of emitted particles remaining airborne within the room by
up to 70%; and (2) positioning HCWs facing the opposite direction to the main air flow would
reduce their exposure.
Conclusions: This study documented the presence of SARS -CoV-2 among HCWs in a neg -
ative pressure ICU room of an infected patient with or without the use of an SGCG. The
simulation will help to improve the design of the SGCG and the positioning of HCWs in the
room.

Introduction

The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID -19) pandemic, caused by severe acute
respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV- 2), has affected more than 760 million people
worldwide, with 6.9 million deaths as of 1st June 2023 [1]. The contagiousness of SARS-CoV-
2 is associated with the emission of viral aerosols by infectious patients, and by the fact that
they can remain viable and infectious for hours and even days on surfaces [2,3]. The risk of
healthcare workers (HCWs) developing infectious diseases because o f contact with patients is
well recognized [4] and increased during the COVID-19 pandemic [4-6].
Aerosol-generating procedures (AGPs) may increase the exposure of HCWs to
airborne infectious agents [7,8], although there is a lack of evidence on the subject [9]. AGPs,
along with normal respiratory activities such as breathing and coughing, lead to the shedding
of airborne particles into the environment, and these can be virus -laden when emitted by an
infectious patient [10]. The diameter of airborne particles ranges between 100 nm and 1 mm
(droplets) before evaporating and forming a droplet nuclei or ae rosol [11,12]. It is considered
that particles with diameter <10 mm can remain airborne and initiate infection at both short and
long distances and can propagate further than 1 m from the source, remaining infectious in the
air for up to 3h [2,10]. High-risk AGPs are considered to be those that involve the manipulation
of high viral load tissues, such as endotracheal intubation or extubation, airway suctioning,
gastric tube insertion and non -invasive ventilation [13 , 15]. However, a recent study showed
that upper airway suctioning was not associated with a higher aerosol concentration, and this
was actually lower compared with breathing and coughing [16].
As a result, clinicians have developed protective devices, such as the SplashGuard
Caregiver (SGCG), with the aim of minimizing the exposure of HCWs to aerosols during
AGPs, thus providing more freedom to perform these AGPs. The SGCG was proposed as a
redesigned ‘aerosol box’, originally invented by a Taiwanese anaesthesiologist (Figure 1) [17-
19]. It consists of a large Plexiglas box installed above the patient’s head and torso that contains
six doors for simultaneous access by HCWs [18,19]. These openings have optional press -fit
plugs and a high -efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter, allowing them to be connected to
continuous suction to create a negative environment, which provides an extra shield to minimize
the spread of viral particles. Some reports described that the SGCG can reduce the exposure of
HCWs to virus during endotracheal intubation in the operating theatre, and suctioning in the
emergency room [15,20,21].

43
The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of the SGCG prototype on the
presence of viral particles on HCWs’ foreheads, and in the air near HCWs responsible for
treating patients hospitalized with COVID -19 in an intensive care unit (ICU). Furthermore, it
was proposed that the movement of aerosols produced by a patient in an ICU room should be
modelled using three-dimensional (3D) computational fluid dynamics (CFD) [20] to simulate
air flow as well as the movement of numerous airborne particles prod uced by a patient’s
respiratory activity (conventional breathing and coughing), with and without the use of the
SGCG. From this, the impact of each scenario on the local concentration of potentially virus -
laden airborne particles can be better understood, as it is essential to find ways to mitigate risks
for frontline workers.

Methods
A prospective single-center cohort study was undertaken from April to June 2021. The
study included patients admitted to an ICU, who tested positive for COVID -19, and HCWs.
The primary outcome was evidence of a decrease in the proportion of active SARS-CoV-2 viral
particles in samples collected from HCWs’ foreheads and in the patient’s environment among
those who used the SGCG during AGPs. Regardless of whether or not an SGCG was used, all
HCWs wore the personal protective equipment (PPE) recommended by the World Health
Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during an AGP, which
included N95 respirator, gown, gloves, eye protection (goggles or face shield) and apron. AGPs
include endotracheal intubation/extubation, oropharyngeal or endotracheal aspiration, gas tric
tube placement, use of nasal cannula in spontaneous breathing, ventilatory assistance with high-
flow nasal cannula, and other non -invasive ventilation [13]. The study was approved by the
Ethics Committee of Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Sainte-Justine (No. MP-21- 2020-2870),
and all patients provided written informed consent prior to inclusion in the study.
In a second step, a 3D CFD model [22] was made of an ICU room containing a virtual
patient with and without an SGCG during normal breathing or coughing. This considered all
morphological characteristics of the ICU room in terms of ventilation (negative pre ssure,
temperature, inlet/outlet positions and mass flow rates) and architecture (exact room
dimensions and geometry, door position, patient position and additional unit particularities).
The 3D CFD model is able to evaluate the local concentration of part icles present in the
environment over time, considering their size (droplets and aerosols), initial position and
spreading velocity (normal breathing or coughing), and environmental factors such as the air
flow induced by the room’s ventilation system. A commercial Lattice Boltzmann-based method
code, PowerFLOW [23], was used to run the numerical simulations and generate numerical
results. The underlying principles of this technique have been described in detail by Crawford
et al. [22].

Protective measure against aerosols of viral particles (Figure 1): The SGCG is an acrylic
box, placed over the patient’s head and upper torso. It contains six different access doors (two
at the front and two on each side) which allows several HCWs to perform procedures related to
the upper airways simultaneously, while limiting the amount and distance of infected particles
projected into the environment. In addition, two smaller semicircular openings on the side allow
the introduction of the breathing circuit and suction equipment, as well as the oxygen tubing
for bag-valve-mask ventilation or the non-rebreather mask. To provide extra protection against

45
aerosolization, in the absence of procedures, shutters occlude the orifices, and a plastic film
covers the rest of the patient’s torso/pelvis for additional sealing. The shutters have optional
press-fit plugs with a HEPA filter that can be connected to a negative pressure suction system,
leading the air from inside the SGCG to the usual medical gas exhaust duct. Finally, the SGCG
has six anchor points on the base, which provides more stability. The user manual detailing the
use of the SGCG (Class 1 reusable medical device) can be consulted using the following link:
https://rsr-qc.ca/Splashguard-cg/.

Virus detection: Environmental sampling for SARS -CoV-2 was performed using personal
pumps and sampling cassettes: (1) in the amb ient air before the AGP; (2) in the air of patients
inside the SGGC; (3) in the air 1 m from the patient after the AGP; and (4) through a swab on
the forehead of each HCW after an AGP. The techniques performed for viral detection are
detailed below.
- Air samples: Stationary and personal air samples were collected using Institute of
Occupational Medicine (IOM) air samplers loaded with 25 -mm gelatin filters (SKC,
Eighty Four, PA, USA). For stationary samples, a flow rate of 10 L/min was achieved
using a calibrated regulator connected to suction present in the room [24]. Personal
samples were collected at a flow rate of 3 L/min using a GilAir Plus Personal Air
Sampling Pump (Sensidyne, Saint Petersburg, FL, USA). After collection, gelatin filters
were dismounted from the IOM devices, solubilized in 2 mL of Gibco’s viral transport
medium (VTM; ThermoFisher, Winnipeg, Canada), and stored at -80oC until analysis.
- Swab samples The forehead of each HCW was swabbed using a HydraFlock 600 sterile
flock swab (Puritan, Guilford, ME, USA) at the end of treatment. Swab samples were
eluted in 1 mL of VTM and stored at -80oC until analysis.
- RNA extraction of samples : RNA was purified using 400 mL of each sample using a
Mag™MAX Viral RNA Isolation Kit (Applied Biosystems, Vilnius, Lithuania).
Purified RNA was eluted in 50 mL of elution buffer and stored at -80oC until
quantification. A no template control was performed for each lot of samples threated.
- Quantitative PCR: Briefly, each sample was amplified in triplicate, targeting ORF1b of
the SARS-CoV-2 genome. Viral genome quantities were estimated by averaging the
results of all replicates based on a ORF1b plasmid standard curve with a lower limit of
detection of 1 plasmid per quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR),
corresponding to a cycle threshold value of 38. The protocol has been described in detail
elsewhere [24,25].

46

3D computational fluid dynamics model [22]: The simulations were based on the digital twin
of the same patient room in which the samples were taken, as described above. It includes the
room furniture and devices in place, including the bed, as well as the position of the HCW. The
ventilation details were also reproduced based on the technical specifications (Figure 2A), with
an air mass flow outlet at the center of the room, above the bed, which extracts 1410 m3/h from
the room. A secondary outlet is locate d in the bathroom and extracts 168 m 3/h. These airflow
rates were measured directly at each ventilation vent by the facilities department using an
anemometer. In addition, an inlet is located above the main door and allows 935 m 3/h of air
inside the room. Finally, a 20-mm gap was modelled between both room doors and the floor in
order to allow air to enter the room from the corridor, and balance the mass flows injected and
extracted from the room. Overall, this corresponded to 11 air changes per hour within this ICU
room. The baseline scenario corresponded to the patient lying on the bed without an SGCG
(Figure 2B). Two modified scenarios were also modelled, corresponding to the same patient
with an SGCG: one with a gap between the plastic film and the Plexiglas box of 140 mm at the
base (Figure 2C); and one with a 20 -mm gap ( Figure 2D). The SGCG was modelled in the
configuration where the negative pressure suction system is active. The patient was modelled
in detail, considering skin temperature as well as a detailed geometry of the upper respiratory
airways of an adult. In all three cases, the distribution of particles dispersed in the environment
by the air flow was analyzed after being shed by the patient’s normal breathing respiratory
activities. The breathing rate was set at 12 L/min and the emission rate was chosen in order to
have a concentration of emitted particles of 100 particles/L [26]. The size distribution used in
the model for these emitted airborne particles, which are considered to be reduced to droplet
nuclei, is a normal distribution centered around 3.2 mm [27]. It was considered that each of
these particles can contain one or more virions and is potentially infectious when inhaled in
sufficiently large quantities. It should also be noted that the use of different oxygen support
devices or the practice of a specific type of AGP were not considered in the simulation, and that
only a standardized adult patient was modelled (no child patient was modelled).

Statistical analysis: Qualitative data are expressed as absolute frequencies (n) and percentages.
Continuous quantitative variables are expressed as medians (minimum and maximum)
considering non-parametric distribution, and analysis was performed using the Mann Whitney
U-test. The qPCR results of patients that used an SGCG and their HCWs were compared with

Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS Version 21.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).

Results
Phase 1 (qPCR analysis): Fourteen batches of samples were included, and 67
analyses were performed in the room with SARS-CoV-2-positive patients. Median age was 11
years (range 1 month - 40 years) and median weight was 54 kg (range 3.5 - 107 kg). Only three
samples were identified as qPCR positive: one in the SCCG group (one of 33 analyses: 3%)
and two in the non -SGCG group (two of 34 analyses: 5.9%). The exposure time of the qPCR
collection devices (pump or swab) did not differ significantly between the groups. On Chi -

were infected. Although feedback was not collected from patients and HCWs about their

Phase 2 (simulation analysis): An aerodynamic analysis was conducted using CFD.
Airflow leakages were observed through the thin gap below the two room doors, due to the
room being under negative pressure ( Figure 3A ). Due to this gap and the position of the
extraction vent of the heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) system above the
patient, air flows enter the room under the two perpendicular room doors, colliding at high
velocities (>1 m/s) before merging and propagating towards the ceiling on the opposite side of
the room.
The SGCG and the patient are in the path of the turbulent flow which forms between
the room doors and the HVAC outlet and deflects towards the ceiling ( Figure 3B ). It is
important to note that this air flow is able to enter the SGCG through the opening created by
the plastic film, creating strong recirculation inside, and can exit through the opposite opening,
near the HCW (Figure 3C,D). The air renewal induced by the suction at the back of the device
is not as efficient as that induced by the air flow pass ing through the opening created by the
plastic film, regardless of the size of the gap (Figure 3C,D).

After performing the aerodynamic simulation and analysis, the particles emitted during
the breathing and coughing cycle were introduced in the simulation and followed. In the first
scenario (no SGCG), the potentially infectious exhaled particles follow the air flow described
in Figure 3C and disperse throughout the room because of the mixing ventilation (Figure 4A).
Over time, these particles are either extracted by the ventilation outlet, deposit on surfaces
(walls, tables, ceiling, medical equipment) or r emain airborne. In the second scenario (SCGC
with a large gap), the emitted particles are trapped and accumulate within the protective device.
However, due to the air flow going through the SGCG, as depicted in Figure 4B, these particles
end up exiting through the opening on the right side of the SGCG, near the HCW. Furthermore,
as the presence of the SGCG reduces the velocity of the air flow that reaches the other side
(<0.4 m/s), the particles entrained stay near the HCW for a longer period (Figure 4B). Finally,
in the third scenario (SGCG with a small gap), the particles tend to remain within the protective
box and only a few escape through the gap. A quantitative analysis is presented in Figure 5,
which represents the cumulative number of particles that go through the orange box modelled
virtually around the HCW ( Figure 4D), located on the left side of the patient. As shown in
Figure 1, the number of particles passing within breathing distance of the HCW was reduced
by 17% when an SGCG (with a gap between the plastic film and the Plexiglas box of 140 mm)
was added compared with the baseline scenario, and reduced by 93% when the gap was reduced
to 20 mm. Thus, placing a HCW behind the patient or to the right would lower their exposure
to higher particle concentrations.

A more detailed analysis was performed in order to better understand the local
dynamics of particle concentrations within the room depending on the scenario, as showcased
in Figure 6. In the baseline configuration, after 100 s of physical time, all the emitted particles
in the room either remained airborne (36%), were extracted efficiently by the ventilation system
(63%) or deposited on surfaces (1%). This shows that the room had good natural ventilation. In
the second configuration (SGCG with 140 -mm gap), over half of the particles shed by the
patient escaped the SGCG and were in the room (58%), which confirms the previous
observations that the air flow within the room tends to enter the SGCG through the gap and exit
on the other side. Overall, the number o f particles remaining airborne in the room (32%) was
comparable to baseline, whilst a lower amount was extracted (23% through ventilation and 7%
through the SGCG). A large proportion of particles remained airborne within the SGCG (35%).
Finally, the third configuration (SGCG with 20-mm gap) showcases an improved situation as
only 10% of the emitted particles remained airborne in the room after 100 s. Seventy -two
percent of particles remained airborne within the SGCG, and only 14% were extracted by its
ventilation mechanism. It is important to note that the accumulation of aerosols within the
SGCG can become an issue when it is removed after the AGP, as they will be released in the
room’s environment. When analyzing the air flow within the SGCG, it can be hypothesized that
increasing the air suction rate of its negative pressure suction system could lead to improved
extraction of airborne particles within the SGCG and a lower concentration in the room.

Discussion
Despite the use of PPE and the SGCG, HCWs are susceptible to contamination by
viruses, given their continuous presence in the environment, as demonstrated by the viral
detection analysis developed, and regardless of the use or not of the SGCG. From this, t he
aerosolization simulation of the airborne particles aimed to delineate the spread of the virus in
the room and identify measures that could be effective in reducing the risk of contamination.
This showed that: (1) reducing the gap between the plastic fi lm and the Plexiglas box may
decrease the number of particles remaining in the room air significantly (70% less after 100 s);
and (2) depending on the room architecture and ventilation design, the position of the HCW
could be important in reducing exposure to airborne pathogens.
Despite the adaptations developed in the SGCG, the presence of particles in the
environment was observed by viral analysis and by simulation with a common SGCG
configuration (gap of 140 mm). From the 3D simulation, it was observed that in the presence
of an SGCG with a 140-mm gap, over half (58%) of the particles shed by the patient escape the
SGCG and go into the room. In comparison, with a gap of 20 mm, only 10% of particles go
into the room air and 72% remain airborne inside the SGCG, showing that reduci ng the gap
seems to be important to improve the protective efficiency of the SGCG. It should also be
emphasized that there is a high concentration of particles inside the SGCG, so their
removal/movement from the room must be done carefully to avoid spreading them in room air.
CFD simulation has been widely employed as a fast, reliable and cost -effective
technique to support decision making and predict mitigation protocols. Its combination with
clinical data has optimal applicability, and this was proposed in this study. Physica l
measurements (phage or gas tracer) to correlate with the CFD analysis were not performed and
would add value. Based on this, it was possible to verify that the traditional positioning of the
HCW, facing the door and therefore facing the air stream, could expose them to a larger amount
of virus and possible contamination. However, with the HCW’s back turned towards the door,
this exposure could be reduced, even if this higher exposure was not reflected in contamination
levels through the sampling, as none of the HCWs evaluated were infected by SARS -CoV-2.
This is due to the fact that it is not only the presence of airborne virus which determines
infection. The use of PPE, the type of AGP performed (e.g. intubation and positive pressure
ventilation seem to b e riskier), the duration of exposure of the HCW to the pathogen, their
immune status, the clinical condition of the patient and the virulence of the strain can also have
an impact [28e30].

54
Over the course of the pandemic, the science around the modes of transmission of
SARS-CoV-2 has evolved, with increasing recognition that transmission occurs through
multiple modes of contact with particles of varying sizes. However, the relative contribution of
each mode of transmission, and how it may vary according to the environment and circum -
stances is not well delineated [29,31]. In the present study, the use of PPE probably explains
the lack of contamination of the HCWs. However, at the beginning of the pandemic, shortages
in PPE were observed at some centers, and HCW positioning combined with SGCG use could
have been an option to limit HCW exposure to viral particles. It is important to note that
patients’ needs were assessed carefully before the device was implemented, and a user manual
was drawn up to preve nt any misuse, including management of the device in emergency
situations (available at https://rsr-qc.ca/Splashguard-cg/ with English and French versions). No
side effects were recorded during the use of the device.
The COVID-19 pandemic resulted in the implementation of several public health and
social measures to mitigate spread, which have likely contributed to the significant reduction in
seasonal respiratory viruses such as influenza and respiratory syncytial vir us in Canada [32],
the USA [28] and Europe [33]. Therefore, while these measures were evaluated in the con- text
of SARS-COV-2, they are certainly transposable to other etiological agents. For example, since
the decline of the SARS - COV-2 pandemic, there h as been a major increase in respiratory
syncytial infection in paediatrics, and use of the same virus containment measures adopted
during the COVID-2 pan- demic could be explored [34,35].
The strengths of this study include its prospective design and a pragmatic approach to
viral spread, from detection of the virus by accurate methods to the simulation of aerosolized
particles within a patient room. In addition, the use of a single room for both virus collection
and simulation, addressing all details of its architecture and ventilation, helped to reduce
evaluation biases.
Limitations of this study include the single-centre design, the lack of characterization
of the strain’s virulence, and the small number of patients and AGPs included. Furthermore,
based on the viral PCR results, as well as the CFD simulation method (exper imental), it was
not fully demonstrated that the SGCG offered additional protection over standard PPE. How -
ever, by adjusting the device in the CFD (narrowing the gap), the authors were able to identify
recommendations for making better use of the SGCG.
In conclusion, this study documented the presence of SARS - CoV-2 in the
environment of infected patients without HCW contamination. This indicates that other
variables are associated with contamination, as well as the presence of the virus in the air.

55
Furthermore, the simulation showed that reducing the gap between the plastic film and the
Plexiglas box, and modifying the suction port design would make the SGCG more effective.
Finally, the position of the HCW within the room can have an impact on their exposure to
airborne pathogens.

7 CONCLUSÕES

Esta tese demonstrou que a integração entre a mecânica respiratória e a biossegurança
é essencial para o manejo das disfunções respiratórias agudas em UTIP. Os dados obtidos neste
estudo nos permitem concluir que:

1. A caracterização da mecânica respiratória em lactentes com disfunção respiratória aguda
grave evidenciou elevada resistência das vias aéreas e redução moderada da complacência,
configurando um padrão fisiopatológico predominantemente obstrutivo;
2. A discrepância entre PIP e PPLAT mostrou -se diretamente relacionada ao aumento da
resistência do sistema respiratório e às constantes de tempo prolongadas, evidenciando
limitações no uso isolado da PIP para ajuste ventilatório;
3. O modelo experimental in vitro apresentou baixa acurácia clínica para estimar a PPLAT a
partir da PIP em lactentes com infecção viral grave, não sendo confiável para aplicação isolada
à beira-leito;
4. O uso do dispositivo SGCG associou -se à redução da dispersão de partículas virais e da
exposição ocupacional durante PGA em ambiente de terapia intensiva;
5. As simulações por CFD demonstraram que a vedação adequada do dispositivo e o
posicionamento dos profissionais em na direção oposta ao fluxo principal de ar ambiente
reduzem significativamente a concentração de aerossóis no ambiente e;
6. A integração dos achados clínicos e das simulações permitiu propor um modelo prático de
manejo ventilatório que concilia a oferta de tratamento ao paciente e a segurança da equipe
multiprofissional.

59
8 CONSIDERAÇÕES FINAIS

Os resultados apresentados ampliam o campo de investigação e apontam para
desdobramentos relevantes em pesquisas futuras, incluindo:

1. A avaliação do impacto – em termos de tempo de VM ou morbimortalidade – da aplicação
da mecânica respiratória em diferentes cenários pediátricos como uma ferramenta de apoio à
tomada de decisão clínica relacionada ao desmame ventilatório ou à modificação de estratégias
ventilatórias;
2. A avaliação da mecânica respiratória em pacientes em respiração espontânea, com ênfase na
mensuração do esforço inspiratório, atualmente reconhecido como importante determinante
para VILI e;
3. C ontinuidade na investigação de dispositivos de contenção de aerossóis , bem como o
aprofundamento das análises aerodinâmicas em ambientes hospitalares.

Tais desdobramentos reforçam o mérito e a relevância deste trabalho, evidenciando
seu potencial de continuidade e sua contribuição para o avanço do conhecimento e para a
qualificação da assistência em UTIP.

8.1 Framework conceitual

Com base nos achados desta tese e na literatura sobre mecânica respiratória e controle
de infecção em unidades de terapia intensiva, propõe -se um framework conceitual que integra
avaliação fisiológica do sistema respiratório com estratégias de biossegurança. Esse modelo
busca orientar a tomada de decisão clínica em cenários de disfunções respiratórias agudas,
conciliando a individualização da ventilação mecâ nica com a redução do risco de exposição
ocupacional. Os dois eixos adotados são: (1) adequação fisiológica da ventilação, guiada por
parâmetros de mecânica respiratória; e (2) redução do risco de exposição ocupacional, guiada
por medidas de biossegurança proporcionais ao risco de aerossolização, conforme ANEXO 2.

RESUMO

Introdução: As disfunções respiratórias agudas figuram entre as principais causas de
internação em Unidades de Terapia Intensiva Pediátrica (UTIP), correspondendo a mais de um
terço das admissões e configurando-se como a forma mais prevalente de falência orgânica em
crianças criticamente enfermas. O manejo dessas condições requer domínio da mecânica
respiratória e rigor na adoção de medidas de biossegurança, especialmente em contextos de alta
transmissibilidade viral, como durante a pandemia de COVID -19. Objetivos: Integrar os
princípios da mecânica respiratória e d e biossegurança no manejo de disfunções respiratórias
agudas em UTIP, buscando estratégias que otimizem a ventilação mecânica e reduzam o risco
ocupacional para a equipe multiprofissional. Métodos: Esta tese foi composta por dois estudos
complementares. O primeiro, de caráter observacional retrospectivo, foi conduzido na UTIP do
Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre (Brasil) e incluiu 37 lactentes, de 1 a 24 meses, com
insuficiência respiratória associada a infecção viral grave e submetidos à ventilação mecânica
invasiva. O objetivo foi avaliar a relação entre a pressão inspiratória de pico (PIP) e a pressão
de platô (PPLAT), bem como a precisão de um modelo preditivo para estimativa de PPLAT a partir
da PIP. O segundo estudo, prospectivo e de coorte, foi realizado no Hospital Sainte -Justine
(Canadá) e avaliou a eficácia do dispositivo SplashGuard Caregiver (SGCG) na redução da
dispersão de aerossóis durante procedimentos geradores de aerossóis (PGA) realizados em
pacientes com COVID-19. A análise envolveu a detecção de partículas virais no ambiente e na
face de profissionais expostos a situações de alta transmissibilidade viral, sendo
complementado por simulações de dinâmica de fluidos computacional ( CFD - computational
fluid dynamycs) para analisar o comportamento aerodinâmico destas partículas. Resultados:
No primeiro estudo, observou -se que a PIP superestimou significativamente PPLAT, com
diferença média de 7,3 ± 4 cmH₂O (p < 0,01), evidenciando as limitações de modelos preditivos
baseadas apenas na PIP em lactentes com elevada resistência de vias aéreas. No segundo, a
detecção de partículas virais reduziu de 5,9% na ausência do SGCG para 3% com o uso do
dispositivo. As simulações CFD demonstraram redução de até 70% na concentração de
aerossóis suspensos no ar quando mantidas aberturas mínimas no SGCG e que o
posicionamento dos profissionais de saúde n o sentido oposto ao principal fluxo de ar do
ambiente pode promover redução adicional da exposição. Conclusões: A integração entre os
princípios da mecânica respiratória e da biossegurança fortalece a qualidade da assistência em
UTIP, favorecendo o desenvolvimento de estratégias ventilatórias mais seguras e
individualizadas, além de contribuir para a mitigação dos riscos ocupacionais.
